summary: This document describes a DHCPv4 option for exchanging information about a client's fully qualified domain name and about who is responsible for updating the DNS records related to the client's address assignment.

eli5.summary: When your computer gets an address, it can also say what name it would like, and the server and computer agree who should update the DNS phone book.

questions: who updates dns for dhcp clients
what is the dhcp client fqdn option
what do the s o n e bits mean in client fqdn
subtitle: How a DHCPv4 client and server agree on the client's name and on who updates its DNS records.

tldr.problem: When a host gets an address by DHCP, DNS needs matching A and PTR records, and someone has to decide who updates them and what name the host uses.
tldr.mechanism: The Client FQDN option (code 81) carries the client's full or partial domain name plus flag bits. Those bits let the client say whether it or the server should update the A record, or that the server should do no updates at all, and let the server reply with what it will do.
tldr.outcome: The option only negotiates the name and who does the updates. Local policy, DNS update security and name conflict handling are left to other mechanisms.

facts.label: Flags field
facts.value: 1 octet: MBZ, N, E, O, S

today: RFC 4702 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2006. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the available metadata. Name conflicts are covered separately in RFC 4703.

sections.title: Names, Addresses and DHCP
sections.content:
DNS keeps the mapping between a host's fully qualified domain name (FQDN) and its IP address in two kinds of resource records: A and PTR. DNS update (RFC 2136) lets those records be changed over the network. DHCPv4 (RFC 2131) gives a client its address and other configuration.

This document defines the Client FQDN option so that DHCP clients and servers can exchange information about the client's FQDN and about who is responsible for updating the A and PTR records. It applies only to DHCP client and server processes, not to other processes that start DNS updates.
sections.eli5: The town phone book maps names to house numbers. This option lets a new house and the address helper decide who writes the entry.

sections.title: Who Updates Which Record
sections.content:
Two separate DNS updates may happen when a client gets an address: one for the A record (name to address) and one for the PTR record (address to name). The option is mainly meant for two cases: the client updates the A record and the server updates the PTR record, or the server updates both.

The reason is authority. A client may be given authority over its own A records, or that authority may be limited to a server so a client cannot list arbitrary addresses or names. The only reasonable place for authority over the PTR records is the DHCP server that allocates the address. A third case is also supported: the client asks the server to do no updates, which is presumed rare because of the authority issues.

Whether clients and servers may update zones is local policy. The document requires no specific policy and proposes none.
sections.eli5: Either the new house writes its own name in the phone book and the helper writes the reverse entry, or the helper writes both. Which is allowed depends on the local rules.

sections.title: The Client FQDN Option
sections.content:
The option has code 81. Len counts the octets after the Len field and is at least 3. After that come a one-octet Flags field, two one-octet RCODE fields and the Domain Name. A client MAY send the option in both DHCPDISCOVER and DHCPREQUEST. If it sends it in DHCPDISCOVER, it MUST send it in later DHCPREQUEST messages, though the contents MAY change. Only one such option MAY appear in a message, and implementations MUST support option concatenation (RFC 3396).

The Flags are MBZ (four bits, which senders MUST clear and receivers MUST ignore), then N, E, O and S.

  • S: whether the server SHOULD (1) or SHOULD NOT (0) do the A record update. In a reply, 1 means the server has taken responsibility for it.
  • O: set by a server to 1 when its S bit differs from the client's. A client MUST set it to 0.
  • N: 1 means the server SHOULD NOT perform any DNS updates. If N is 1, S MUST be 0.
  • E: 1 means the name is in canonical DNS wire format; 0 means the deprecated ASCII encoding.

The RCODE1 and RCODE2 fields are deprecated. A client SHOULD set them to 0 and ignore them on receipt. A server SHOULD set them to 255 and MUST ignore them on receipt. They were originally used to report the DNS response codes for A and PTR updates, and are kept because the option was already in wide use.
sections.eli5: The option is a little form with a few tick boxes: please you do it, I will do it, do nothing at all, and which way the name is written.

sections.title: The Domain Name Field
sections.content:
The Domain Name carries all or part of the client's FQDN. It SHOULD be in canonical wire format as in RFC 1035, with the E bit set to 1, and servers MUST support this. Client and server MUST NOT change the contents unless the FQDN has actually changed.

A fully qualified name ends with the terminating zero-length label. A partial name leaves that label off, which tells the server the client knows only part of its name. A client MAY leave the field empty if it wants the server to supply a name.

Some clients implemented an earlier draft that used an ASCII encoding (E bit 0). That use SHOULD be considered deprecated. A server that is not prepared to return ASCII encoding MUST ignore a Client FQDN option with E set to 0, and a server that does answer MUST use the same encoding as the client.
sections.eli5: The name can be written in full, written only in part, or left blank so the helper picks one. The old plain-letters way of writing is being retired.

sections.title: What the Client Does
sections.content:
A client has three choices.

  • Update its own A record: it MUST include the option in DHCPREQUEST, with S, O and N all 0. After it gets a DHCPACK it MAY update the A record unless the server set S to 1.
  • Delegate to the server: it SHOULD include the option in DHCPREQUEST with S set to 1 and O and N set to 0.
  • Ask for no server updates: it sets N to 1 and S and O to 0, and may then do its own updates if the server's N bit is 1.

A client that sends the Client FQDN option MUST NOT also send the Host Name option. A client that delegates updates gets no indication whether the server succeeded, but MAY check with a DNS query. A client that updated its own A record SHOULD delete it before sending a DHCPRELEASE, or attempt to delete it before its lease expires if it cannot renew. A client SHOULD NOT update A records if its address is a private address (RFC 1918).
sections.eli5: The computer picks one: write my own entry, please write it for me, or please write nothing. When it leaves, it should erase its entry.

sections.title: What the Server Does
sections.content:
The server starts with S, O and N at 0 in its reply and copies the client's E bit. If the client's N bit is 1 and the server's configuration allows it, the server sets N to 1. Otherwise, if the client's S bit is 1 and the server allows it, it sets S to 1. If the server's S does not match the client's, it sets O to 1.

The server MAY use the client's name, modify it or substitute a different one, and SHOULD send its notion of the complete FQDN. If the client sends both Client FQDN and Host Name, the server SHOULD ignore Host Name.

The server SHOULD NOT do any updates if N is 1 in the DHCPACK, and SHOULD delete records it previously added. It MAY do the PTR update unless N is 1, and MAY do the A update if S is 1. It MUST NOT start DNS updates when answering a DHCPDISCOVER. When a lease expires or is ended early, the server SHOULD delete the PTR record it added, and the A record too if it was responsible for it.
sections.eli5: The helper reads the form, says yes or no to each request and ticks a box if it changed the answer. It only writes in the phone book once the address is really given, and erases entries when the address is returned.

sections.title: DNS Record Lifetimes and Conflicts
sections.content:
Records tied to DHCP clients are more volatile than static ones. The TTL on a DNS record added SHOULD NOT exceed 1/3 of the lease time, but SHOULD NOT be less than 10 minutes. Administrators should be able to configure TTLs and their bounds, as an absolute interval or a percentage of the lease time.

The document does not say how to prevent name conflicts. It notes that conflicts cannot occur if only one updater holds a security token for a name, or if names are based on the bound address. Otherwise, a conflict resolution technique such as the one in RFC 4703 SHOULD be used.
sections.eli5: Entries for visitors should expire quickly, because visitors leave. Two houses must not claim the same name, so some other rule has to prevent that.

sections.title: Security of DNS Updates
sections.content:
Unauthenticated DNS updates can cause great confusion through attack or misconfiguration. Administrators need to be wary of unsecured updates to zones exposed to the global Internet, and clients and servers should use origin authentication such as Secure DNS Dynamic Update (RFC 3007).

Whether the client or the server updates the A record is a site-local matter, likely driven by the DNS security model. DHCP itself has no entity authentication, so a server rarely knows a client's identity with confidence. The RFC gives two settings with extra assurance: a cable modem head-end that prevents MAC address spoofing, and a network access server using PPP that encodes client identity in the client-id option. It also says that proper conflict resolution is critical.
sections.eli5: If anyone could write in the phone book, it would be chaos. The helper needs a good way to tell who it is really talking to before it writes a name for them.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: MBZ, N, E, O and S bits.

fields.name: Domain Name
fields.desc: All or part of the client FQDN; variable length.

items.label: Server updates A
items.desc: 1: server SHOULD do the A record update. 0: it SHOULD NOT.

items.label: Override
items.desc: Server sets 1 if its S differs from the client's. Clients set 0.

items.label: No updates
items.desc: 1: server SHOULD NOT do any DNS updates. If 1, S MUST be 0.

items.label: Must be zero
items.desc: Senders clear these bits; receivers ignore them.
